properties.description: The Grand Budapest Hotel (2014), directed by Wes Anderson and featuring Ralph Fiennes, F. Murray Abraham, and Mathieu Amalric, is a comedy-drama adventure set across multiple eras of a once-grand European hotel. Framed as a nested tale, it follows a legendary concierge and his young lobby boy through a caper involving a stolen painting, an inheritance dispute, and a murder, all against the rise of war and social change. The film pairs Anderson's signature visual precision—pastel palettes, miniature-like sets, and exacting symmetry—with a bittersweet meditation on nostalgia, loyalty, and the decay of an era.

properties.description: Grand Hotel (1932), directed by Edmund Goulding and featuring Greta Garbo, John Barrymore and Joan Crawford, is an MGM ensemble drama that adapts Vicki Baum's novel and its stage version by William A. Drake. Set in a luxurious Berlin hotel, the film interweaves multiple guests' stories—romance, debt, theft, and despair—into a bittersweet portrait of loneliness and fleeting human connection. Lavish Art Deco production values and star-centered performances give the picture a polished, theatrical sheen while exploring themes of class, mortality and redemption.

properties.description: Grand Hotel Excelsior (1982), directed by Franco Castellano and Giuseppe Moccia, is an Italian ensemble comedy starring Adriano Celentano, Enrico Montesano, and Carlo Verdone. Set over a busy summer at a grand seaside hotel, the film follows the manager, a lovestruck guest, a boxer with a big match, a would-be magician attempting a public levitation, and a waiter maintaining a reassuring pretence for his daughter. Through interlocking comic episodes it explores themes of romance, ambition and social pretence with a playful, farcical tone.

properties.description: Week-End at the Waldorf (1945), directed by Robert Z. Leonard, is an MGM ensemble comedy-drama with musical touches starring Ginger Rogers, Lana Turner and Walter Pidgeon, among others. Set over a weekend in a luxury Manhattan hotel, the film follows multiple interlocking stories—romantic entanglements, comic cases of mistaken identity and quieter threads of guilt and duty against a wartime backdrop. The tone mixes sophisticated repartee, sentimental emotion and light musical spectacle, reflecting escapist studio entertainment of the era.

properties.description: Hotel (1967), directed by Richard Quine and starring Rod Taylor, Catherine Spaak, and Karl Malden, is a Technicolor drama set in a storied New Orleans grand hotel. As debts mount and a takeover looms, the owner, manager, staff, and a rotating cast of guests contend with crimes, cover-ups, and personal reckonings across one eventful day. The film interweaves character-driven vignettes—featuring a hit-and-run cover-up, a cat burglar’s antics, and corporate machinations—to examine nostalgia, institutional decline, and moral compromise, all underscored by a lush, jazz-tinged score.
